name: The Mouth of the Lachine
description: Shot on salvaged optical hardware over fourteen months in the drowned industrial fringe south of the Milwaukee Shelf, this flat-screen film follows three generations of a Haitian-Ukrainian family who have lived beneath the same corrugated overhang since the city's expansion consumed their neighborhood. Director Ama Desrosiers-Kovalenko refused all licensing offers and distributed physical copies via courier networks. It has no score — only ambient industrial sound recorded on location.
cultural_impact: Became a touchstone for the Shelf documentary movement and is taught — illegally — in several underground school networks as an example of pre-corponation filmmaking ethics.
story_hooks: A physical copy of the film is hidden inside a wall of the family home depicted — the family still lives there and doesn't know.
Desrosiers-Kovalenko disappeared eight months after the film's release; her final footage has never been found.
A Tier 3 film studies professor is fired for screening the film, triggering a student movement that escalates unexpectedly.
